title: Pancreatic Enzymes: Lipase Lingers, Amylase Wanders
summary: Use lipase and amylase correctly in suspected acute pancreatitis — the 2-of-3 diagnostic rule, enzyme timing for late presenters, why enzyme levels don’t grade severity, and how to recognise macroamylasemia.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 23 Hit 1 (lipase vs amylase kinetics), Hit 2 (diagnostic criteria; enzymes not linked to severity), Hit 3 (macroamylasemia), Trap 1 and the Figure 23 anchor. Checked against Sadaria 2026, Varlamov 2026, Lázár 2026, Dimitrovska-Ivanova 2026 and Choi 2023. Hit 2 updated to the revised Atlanta 2-of-3 rule (register flag rv-ap-criteria). Not taught: the reviewer’s 8–14-day lipase duration, 48–72-h amylase normalisation (source read: 3–5 days) and 10–20× ULN amylase peak.

objectives: State the revised Atlanta criteria for acute pancreatitis.
Compare lipase and amylase kinetics and specificity.
Explain why enzyme levels do not grade severity.
Recognise macroamylasemia from serum, urine and clearance findings.

scenes.title: Amylase normal on day 4 — pancreatitis ruled out?
scenes.altText: A patient arrives on day 4 of epigastric pain radiating to the back. Amylase card: normal. Lipase card: 6× the upper limit. A second card: an asymptomatic man with amylase 3× high for months, lipase normal. Question token: “Which numbers matter?”

cues.text: A woman arrives on the fourth day of severe upper abdominal pain that bores into her back. Her amylase is normal.
Her lipase is six times the upper limit. Meanwhile, a healthy man has had a high amylase for months — with a normal lipase.
Which enzyme should you trust — and when does a high amylase mean nothing at all?

scenes.title: Normal: where amylase and lipase come from
scenes.altText: A pancreas card releases two enzyme tokens (amylase and lipase) into the duodenum. A salivary-gland card also releases amylase. Normally only a little of each leaks into the blood. Amylase is normally cleared by the kidney into urine (arrow to a kidney card).

cues.text: The pancreas makes digestive enzymes, including amylase for starch and lipase for fat, and pours them into the gut.
Amylase isn’t only pancreatic — the salivary glands make it too. Lipase is far more pancreas-specific.
Normally, only a small amount of each leaks into the blood, so serum levels stay low.
The kidneys normally clear amylase into the urine — which matters for one classic trap.

scenes.title: What changes in acute pancreatitis
scenes.altText: A timeline chart (days 0–7). Two bars per day: amylase rises early and falls back to normal by about day 3–5; lipase rises within 4–8 hours, peaks around 24 h, and stays high longer. A criteria card (revised Atlanta): at least two of three — typical abdominal pain; amylase and/or lipase ≥ 3 × ULN; characteristic imaging. A caveat token: enzyme height does not predict severity.

cues.text: When acinar cells are injured, enzymes pour into the blood. Lipase rises within four to eight hours and peaks at about a day.
Amylase rises too, but falls fast — it can be back to normal within three to five days, even while the pancreas is still inflamed. Lipase stays up longer, so it’s better for late presenters.
The diagnosis needs two of three: typical abdominal pain, amylase or lipase at least three times the upper limit, or characteristic imaging.
And the height of the enzyme doesn’t predict how sick the patient will get. Severity is judged by organ failure and complications — not by lipase.

scenes.title: In the lab: when a high amylase misleads
scenes.altText: Card: amylase is not specific — salivary disease, bowel obstruction or ischemia, renal failure and gynecologic conditions also raise it; amylase may be only mildly raised in alcohol- or triglyceride-induced pancreatitis. Macroamylasemia: amylase bound to IgA or IgG forms a complex too large to be filtered by the kidney — serum amylase chronically high, urine amylase low, amylase-to-creatinine clearance ratio low (< 1%); lipase normal. An amylase complex token is shown too big to pass a kidney filter.

cues.text: Amylase is a noisy marker. Salivary gland disease, bowel obstruction or ischemia, kidney failure and gynecologic problems can all raise it.
It can also stay deceptively low — in pancreatitis caused by alcohol or very high triglycerides, amylase may be only mildly raised or even normal.
Then there’s macroamylasemia: amylase bound to an immunoglobulin forms a complex too big for the kidney to filter. Serum amylase stays high for months, but urine amylase is low.
The clue: a low amylase-to-creatinine clearance ratio — under one percent — with a normal lipase and a well patient.

props.label: Alcohol / ↑TG pancreatitis: amylase may be normal

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Order amylase and lipase together for accuracy” is crossed out → “Lipase alone is preferred; amylase adds little.” Trap card: “Normal amylase on day 4 rules out pancreatitis” is crossed out → “Amylase falls fast; lipase stays high longer.” Trap card: “The higher the lipase, the sicker the patient” is crossed out → “Enzyme level doesn’t predict severity.”

cues.text: Trap one: ordering both enzymes rarely helps. Lipase alone is the preferred test; amylase is no longer recommended on its own.
Trap two: a normal amylase on day four doesn’t rule out pancreatitis. Amylase falls fast; lipase stays up longer.
Trap three: a sky-high lipase doesn’t mean severe pancreatitis. Enzyme levels don’t predict severity.

scenes.title: Lipase lingers; amylase wanders
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Lipase lingers (stays up, pancreas-specific); amylase wanders (falls fast, comes from many places).” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: lipase lingers; amylase wanders. Lipase stays up and stays loyal to the pancreas. Amylase falls fast and comes from many places.
Where it breaks: lipase is more specific, not perfectly specific; neither enzyme measures severity; and reference limits — and so “three times the limit” — depend on the assay.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Acute pancreatitis: 2 of 3 — pain, lipase/amylase ≥ 3 × ULN, imaging · lipase preferred”, “Enzymes don’t grade severity · macroamylasemia: high serum, low urine amylase, normal lipase”.

cues.text: Diagnose acute pancreatitis with two of three criteria, prefer lipase because it is specific and lingers, never grade severity by enzyme height, and recognise macroamylasemia by its low clearance ratio.

props.label: 2 of 3: pain · lipase/amylase ≥ 3 × ULN · imaging — lipase preferred
Enzymes ≠ severity · macroamylasemia: serum ↑, urine ↓, lipase normal

explanation.what: Plain language: lipase is the pancreas’s loyal, long-lasting signal; amylase comes from many places and fades fast; and neither tells you how sick the patient is. Scientific terms: acute pancreatitis = at least two of typical abdominal pain, serum amylase and/or lipase ≥ 3 × ULN, characteristic imaging (revised Atlanta). Lipase rises within 4–8 h and peaks ~24 h; amylase may normalise within 3–5 days. Macroamylasemia = amylase–immunoglobulin complex with reduced renal clearance.
explanation.why: Acinar injury releases enzymes into the blood. Amylase also comes from salivary glands and other tissues, so it is less specific; it clears quickly. Bound to IgA/IgG, amylase cannot be filtered, so serum levels stay high while urine amylase is low.
explanation.measure: Lipase is preferred; amylase is no longer recommended as a standalone diagnostic or prognostic test. Amylase-to-creatinine clearance ratio < 1% with low urine amylase supports macroamylasemia; lipase is normal.
explanation.differs: Lipase (specific, lingers) vs amylase (less specific, falls fast; may be normal in alcohol- or hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis). Pancreatitis vs macroamylasemia (well patient, normal lipase, low clearance ratio).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the 3 × ULN / 2-of-3 rule, the late-presenter trap, “do enzymes predict severity?”, and macroamylasemia patterns.

left.label: Lipase
points: Rises 4–8 h, peaks ~24 h, stays up longer

comparisons.title: Acute pancreatitis vs macroamylasemia
comparisons.distinguisher: Lipase and the amylase clearance ratio.

mnemonic.explanation: Lipase stays elevated and is pancreas-specific; amylase falls quickly and has many sources.
mnemonic.limitation: Lipase is more specific, not perfectly specific; neither enzyme grades severity; “3 × ULN” depends on the assay’s reference limit.

analogyLimitations: Bars are schematic, not measured enzyme curves.
Severity scores, imaging and chronic pancreatitis testing are not covered here.
takeaway: Diagnose acute pancreatitis with two of three criteria, prefer lipase because it is specific and lingers, never grade severity by enzyme height, and recognise macroamylasemia by its low clearance ratio.

questions.stem: A patient presents on day 5 of typical epigastric pain radiating to the back. Amylase is normal; lipase is 5 × ULN. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Consistent with acute pancreatitis; amylase can normalise early while lipase stays elevated
options.rationale: Correct. Typical pain plus lipase ≥ 3 × ULN meets two of three criteria.

options.text: Pancreatitis is excluded because amylase is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Amylase may normalise within 3–5 days.
Incorrect. Lipase stays elevated longer than amylase.

options.text: Imaging is mandatory before any diagnosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Only two of the three criteria are required.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic man has had serum amylase 3 × ULN for six months. Lipase is normal, urine amylase is low, and the amylase-to-creatinine clearance ratio is 0.6%. What is the most likely explanation?

options.rationale: Correct. A large amylase–immunoglobulin complex is not filtered, giving high serum and low urine amylase.
Incorrect. This pattern with a normal lipase and well patient fits macroamylasemia.
Incorrect. There is no pain and lipase is normal.
Incorrect. Renal failure would not give a low clearance ratio with normal kidney function.

questions.stem: Which statement about serum lipase in acute pancreatitis is correct?

options.text: It confirms the diagnosis but does not predict severity
options.rationale: Correct. Lipase levels do not correlate with necrosis or organ failure.

options.text: A higher lipase predicts more severe disease
options.rationale: Incorrect. Enzyme height does not grade severity.

options.text: It peaks within 1 hour of symptom onset
options.rationale: Incorrect. It rises within 4–8 h and peaks around 24 h.

options.text: It is less specific than amylase

claims.text: Revised Atlanta: ≥ 2 of 3 — pain, amylase/lipase ≥ 3 × ULN, imaging.
Lipase rises 4–8 h, peaks ~24 h; amylase may normalise within 3–5 days; lipase more specific and preferred; amylase not recommended standalone.
Neither amylase nor lipase correlates with severity; amylase may be normal in alcohol/hypertriglyceridemia pancreatitis.
Macroamylasemia: Ig-bound amylase, high serum, low urine amylase, ACCR < 1%, normal lipase.
